direction.name: Direction
direction.headline: You are looking for the destination, not the next steps.
paragraphs: Your answers suggest the hard part is not **how** to make a move. It is knowing which move you want. That is why job boards, advice and well-meaning questions have not helped: they all assume you already have an answer.

This is a common place to be after a long run in one role, or a single kind of work. It usually clears faster by looking at what you want more of and less of than by trying to pick a specific job title.
direction.question: What do I want more of, and less of, in the next three years?
direction.exercise: Spend 15 minutes with my Values Finder. It asks what really matters to you at work, which is the best place to start narrowing down your next move.
direction.alsoInTheMix: Some of your answers also point to an open question about **what** you want.

decision.name: Decision
decision.headline: You have the options. Making a trade-off is the hardest part.
paragraphs: You are not short of ideas. Your answers suggest you can see two or three real routes and keep going round them without landing. More research rarely fixes that, because the missing piece is not information.
What usually helps is getting clear on what you are choosing between underneath the options: money against purpose, safety against growth, now against later.
decision.question: What am I really choosing between, underneath the options?
decision.exercise: For each option, write three sentences from yourself two years on: one where it went well, one where it went badly, and one where you never tried. Notice which is hardest to write.
decision.alsoInTheMix: There is also some choosing between options going on.

confidence.name: Confidence
confidence.headline: You know the move. You are not yet backing yourself to make it.
paragraphs: Your answers suggest direction is not the problem. You have a fair idea of what you want. What wobbles is your account of why you are the right person for it, and an inner critic shows up when you have to describe your own value.
This is very common in high performers who have been good at their job for a long time and have never had to sell it. It is a storytelling challenge far more often than a skills gap.
confidence.question: What is the evidence, and how would I say it out loud?
confidence.exercise: Write down three things from the last year that you are proud of. For each, add one line on what was at stake and one on what changed because of **you**. Read them aloud once, then keep the list close for a confidence boost.
confidence.alsoInTheMix: There are also signs you are underselling what you bring.

variants.headline: You have the role. You are not yet backing yourself in it.
paragraphs: Your answers suggest the role itself is not the problem. You were chosen for it. What wobbles is your own account of why you are the right person, and an inner critic shows up when you have to describe your value.
This is very common in high performers who have been good at their job for a long time and are suddenly new at something. It is a storytelling challenge far more often than a skills gap.

transition.name: Transition
transition.headline: You have made the move. Now the job is a different job.
paragraphs: Your answers suggest you are already in it, or about to be, and that much of what secured you the move no longer applies in the same way. That is disorienting for anyone who is used to being good at their work.

The best transitions I have watched are the ones where people decide early what to stop doing, what to keep and what to learn. That works far better than working harder at the old job inside the new one.
transition.question: What do I need to stop doing, now that it is no longer my job?
transition.exercise: Draw three columns: stop, keep and start. List what you did every week in your last role and sort each item into stop or keep. Under start, add three things the new role needs that the old one never asked of you. This is your growth plan, and it will help you focus.
transition.alsoInTheMix: Some of this is also the plain shock of a job that works differently.

momentum.name: Momentum
momentum.headline: You know what to do. It keeps losing to everything else.
paragraphs: Your answers suggest clarity is not what is missing. You have a fair idea of the next step. What is missing is the time, the energy or the deadline that would make it happen, so the day job wins every week.
More effort is rarely the fix. Breaking it down and finding a small first step usually is. Someone to hold you to account helps as well.
momentum.question: What is the smallest version of this I could finish in the next two weeks?
momentum.exercise: Pick the single next action, small enough to finish in an hour. Put it in your calendar this week with a start time, and tell one person you are doing it.
momentum.alsoInTheMix: Time and energy are also getting in the way.

sounding.name: Sounding board
sounding.headline: You are carrying this one on your own.
paragraphs: Your answers suggest you have plenty of thinking and nowhere neutral to do it. The people around you have a stake in what you decide, or you cannot say it out loud at work, so it goes round in your head instead.

A decision made alone is not a worse decision, but it can be a slower and heavier one. Much of the value of a good conversation is hearing yourself say it to someone with nothing riding on the answer.
sounding.question: Who can I think this through with who has nothing riding on my answer?
sounding.exercise: Write the decision as one sentence that starts with "I am deciding whether to". Then record yourself talking it through for five minutes and listen back once. Notice what you said that you had not written down.
sounding.alsoInTheMix: You are also doing a lot of this thinking alone.
